title: What is the future of Earth?
summary: Josh and Chuck speculate on the future of Earth across three time horizons: the next five years, five thousand years, and fifty thousand years. They open with the Kio satellite time capsule project (Jean-Marc Philippe), then cover near-term climate projections (crop yields, coral loss, Arctic ice, sea level rise, water shortages, desertification), Kardashev civilization types (Type I, II, III) with Michio Kaku and Freeman Dyson, transhumanism and life extension (Aubrey de Gray), and the Milankovitch cycles (precession, obliquity, eccentricity) that drive ice ages. They discuss super volcanoes and the Permian-Triassic extinction, and close with a listener email about the whaling ship Essex and cannibalism at sea.

segments.title: Opening banter and the Kio satellite
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode and its three-part structure. Josh describes Ben Bowling's writing on the Kio satellite, a time capsule conceived by French artist Jean-Marc Philippe to be launched into orbit with messages submitted online, a CD-ROM, and DVDs.

segments.title: Framework: humans around or not, and energy use
segments.summary: Josh lays out a choose-your-own-adventure structure: whether humans survive each time period and how advanced technology is. He notes a documentary, Life After People, showing how quickly Earth erases human traces.

segments.title: Near-term climate projections
segments.summary: Chuck reads projections for the coming decades: reduced rainfall and crop yields, world population near 7.6 billion, coral reef losses from warming and acidification, possible ice-free Arctic summers, and water shortages affecting 1.1 to 3.2 billion people. Sources cited include James Overland and Muyin Wang.

segments.title: Sea level rise and desertification
segments.summary: The hosts discuss a one-meter sea level rise and its effects on New York City, the US Southwest, India, Bangladesh and Indonesia, with about 24 million people displaced. They also mention coastal population growth and desertification, and a comparison of CO2 and pH levels with past eras.

segments.title: Next ice age and the carbon dioxide question
segments.summary: Chuck explains that if fossil fuel emissions stopped, CO2 would return to normal and a new ice age could follow in roughly 1,500 years. Josh adds that humans face catastrophic threats such as meteors and ice ages, and that technology must outpace them.

segments.title: Kardashev scale: Type I, II and III civilizations
segments.summary: The hosts describe Nikolai Kardashev's scale, ranking civilizations by energy use. Type I harnesses all planetary energy, per Michio Kaku's estimates of a hundred years. Type II, per Freeman Dyson, would use a star's full output, and Type III would command a galaxy's energy.

segments.title: Transhumanism, Moore's law and life extension
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Moore's law, robotics, transhumanism and genetic engineering. They cite Aubrey de Gray's claim about life extension and funding for anti-aging research, and mention cryonics.

segments.title: Five-thousand and fifty-thousand year outlooks
segments.summary: Robert Lamb's five-thousand-year view is discussed: a Type I outcome could avert ecological disaster, but warfare remains a risk; Type II opens interstellar possibilities. Human divergence from Neanderthals is also mentioned. The hosts then turn to Milankovitch cycles (precession, obliquity, eccentricity) that drive ice ages, and to the next ice age peaking in about 80,000 years.

segments.title: Super volcanoes and mass extinctions
segments.summary: The hosts discuss extinction-level events, including impacts, anoxia and super volcanoes. They describe the Siberian Traps eruption and the Permian-Triassic extinction, which took about 30 million years for Earth to recover from, and mention the film Pierce Brosnan shot about a super volcano.

segments.title: Listener mail: Essex whaling ship cannibalism
segments.summary: A listener, Ashley, writes about the whaleship Essex, which was rammed by a sperm whale, and the survivors who drifted for ninety days and drew lots for cannibalism. The hosts note that the episode on whaling is not yet out and that the story inspired Moby Dick.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts invite listeners to search the website for more on the future of Earth, to send tweets and emails, and close the show.
